Paper [1] (MiniFool) proposes physics-inspired adversarial attacks that minimize a cost combining a χ²-based test statistic based on experimental uncertainties and deviation from a target score, and it is applied in particle/astroparticle settings and also on MNIST and CMS data.

More generally, other constraint-focused adversarial approaches in the list include physics-/constraint-enforcing frameworks such as CAP (which enforces domain-specific feature constraints via an augmented Lagrangian) [3], WAAPO for weather models with channel sparsity/spatial localization/smoothness constraints [4], relational adversarial attacks under integrity constraints [2], and physics-informed adversarial training for neural operators [5].
These differ from [1] by targeting different data/model types and using different constraint mechanisms.

It studies grading label-free multi-topic science exams where a student’s responses to several distinct topics are merged into one big paragraph with no segmentation indicating which span answers which question [1].

It builds reference answers per question, encodes them, constructs a semantic similarity graph over the references, and uses a combination of retrieval/graph traversal and assignment so each question is graded against its corresponding reference answer independently [1].

Relatedly, rubric-anchored grading is emphasized as a key design principle for reliable open-ended grading [2] and for auditable “rubric judge” paradigms [5], though neither specifically targets the “one big paragraph covering multiple questions”/network-of-reference-answers structure described in [1] [2,5].
Paper [9] focuses on AI-assisted scoring for short written texts with human-in-the-loop oversight, but it does not describe the reference-answer network/graph retrieval approach [9].

The closest match is a study on maximizing revenue for batteries and electrolysers by using measured device behavior in Nordic power markets, specifically Danish electricity and ancillary service markets [1].

It explicitly models real hardware characteristics such as ramp limits, efficiency, and setpoint-tracking accuracy, then uses a price-driven optimization framework with real market data to optimize multi-market participation and daily profits [1].

The paper reports optimized daily profits for both a battery energy storage system and an electrolyser, and argues that incorporating experimental performance is important when evaluating business cases across multiple markets and years [1].
The other supplied papers do not address Nordic power exchanges for converter-like tools or electrochemical cells in this way.

One focuses on automated discovery of better reconfigurable power converter topologies, improving figure of merit and efficiency rather than market income optimization [10], while another is about battery power prediction in electric vehicles, not market participation [2].

It uses that state to guide promotion, compression, and eviction, aiming to prevent both forgetting important premises and retaining everything indiscriminately [1].
Other approaches strengthen memories when they help generate a response [2], or track preference strength and evidence while adaptively reinforcing and weakening memories [8].
The matching paper is DeCode: Decoupling Content and Delivery for Medical QA by Po-Jen Ko, Chen-Han Tsai, and Yu-Shao Peng [1].
It presents DeCode, a training-free, model-agnostic framework that adapts existing LLMs to produce contextualized answers in clinical settings by decoupling content and delivery [1].
According to the abstract, DeCode is evaluated on OpenAI HealthBench and improves zero-shot performance from 28.4% to 49.8%, achieving a new state of the art compared to existing methods [1].

Other papers here use knowledge graphs for drug safety tasks, but they are not presented as Hoehndorf’s drug safety knowledge graph.

Dense-to-sparse retrieval is covered in several ways here.

Some papers explicitly convert dense retrievers into sparse ones: Latent Terms shows dense retrievers can be decomposed into BM25-ready sparse features with sparse autoencoders, without sparse supervision or expansion training, and can match or beat the base single-vector scorer [2].

SPLARE likewise uses sparse autoencoders as the basis for learned sparse retrieval, aiming for more structured and expressive sparse features than vocabulary-based methods, with strong multilingual and out-of-domain results [7].
Other papers focus on sparse alternatives that reach dense-like effectiveness or replace dense/multi-vector indexing with sparse coding.
LACONIC is a learned sparse retriever designed to bridge the gap to dense models while using much less index memory [1].
SSR replaces multi-vector dense retrieval and clustering with sparse coding and inverted indexing, improving indexing time, latency, and retrieval quality [10].
Sparse Coverage maps local dense span embeddings to sparse centers for patent retrieval [5].
If you mean combining dense and sparse rather than converting between them, one paper studies tuned dense-sparse fusion for hybrid retrieval [9].
Yes: the matching paper is On the Computational Complexity of Structural Generalization by Zichao Wei [1].

It argues that structural generalization can be formally defined from compositional structure and unbounded generalization, and frames the key complexity result as a gap between an NC^1 lower bound and the learnable ceiling TC^0 of pure Transformers [1].
Under its Montagovian setup, semantic tree evaluation is an NC^1-complete instance, so under the standard assumption TC^0 ≠ NC^1, a pure Transformer cannot learn structural generalization [1].

A related Wei paper is more empirical: Structural Generalization on SLOG without Hand-Written Rules presents a neural cellular automaton with a discrete bottleneck that learns compositional rules from data and achieves strong structural generalization on SLOG without hand-written rules [2].
So [1] is the complexity/theory paper, while [2] studies a learned alternative and analyzes its success and failure patterns on a benchmark [2].

Different retraction maps change stability mainly by changing how an update’s size becomes a rotation angle on the sphere.

The paper says the exponential map is only one choice, and that on the hypersphere the family of retractions differs by this scalar angle rule rather than by the basic norm-preserving geometry; metric projection and Cayley give exact norm-preserving variants, while the identity map and GeoNorm appear only as limits [1].
It also reports that the best validation loss is reached at a finite parameter value, suggesting the exponential map is not the preferred retraction for spherical residual streams [1].

More broadly, the related stability papers show that preserving orthogonality or norm helps training remain stable, while unstable updates come from unconstrained amplification or from gates that reintroduce vanishing gradients [3, 6, 2].
Use explicit temporal metadata and make validity part of retrieval, not just generation.

The papers suggest storing or extracting dates and validity intervals for each item, filtering out invalid or deprecated items before ranking, and then re-ranking with recency or temporal decay so older evidence is trusted less when appropriate [8, 4, 1].

They also suggest checking whether the query actually needs fresh information, since recency requirements vary by question and context; a recency-aware taxonomy can help decide when to retrieve or emphasize newer evidence [3].

If you build and evaluate such a system, be careful: ordinary search-engine date filters can leak post-cutoff information and have unreliable metadata, so frozen time-stamped snapshots or stronger safeguards are safer for retrospective settings [2].
For time-sensitive domains like news, dynamic daily adaptation can improve freshness and relevance over a fixed retriever [7].

The papers differ in approach: Chronofy adds temporal decay and logical validity into representation, retrieval, and reasoning [4], while NuggetIndex uses atomic records with temporal validity intervals and lifecycle states to prevent outdated information from entering ranking [8].

Related papers cover nearby but different tasks.

Another extracts target and stance from Reddit political posts for more granular opinion analysis, using prompting strategies rather than the supervised-fine-tuning-plus-DPO recipe [3].

It also claims that neuro-symbolic systems score well by injecting part of the structure, rather than learning the hard component from finite data.

[2] These two Wei papers differ: [1] is a computational complexity/theory argument about what pure Transformers can learn, while [2] is an empirical/diagnostic study of structural generalization on SLOG without hand-written rules.

[1] Related approaches to improving medical QA with external knowledge include RAG-X, which proposes a diagnostic framework to separately evaluate retrieval vs generation in retrieval-augmented medical QA.

Several papers explicitly introduce a memory “strength” control as part of lifecycle management, but they use it differently.

One paper directly defines strength as an explicit lifecycle state for retention consequence, distinct from confidence or ordinary validity signals, to control promotion, compression, and eviction pressure in persistent memory [1].
Another uses preference memory with explicit strength and evidence tracking, alongside reinforcement, weakening, consolidation, forgetting, and resynthesis in a scheduled lifecycle [8].
Related work controls memory strength more indirectly.
Oblivion strengthens memories that contribute to responses while using decay-driven reductions in accessibility instead of deletion [2].

Other papers frame memory as lifecycle control through consolidation, forgetting, retrieval-driven reconsolidation, or write routing, without specifically centering “strength” as a named state variable [6,7,9].
To make retrieval date-aware, store each fact with its evidence, temporal validity interval, and lifecycle state, then exclude invalid or deprecated facts before ranking [8].
You can also encode fact age in representations, apply time-decay during retrieval, and check whether retrieved evidence is still temporally valid before using it [4].
For time-sensitive questions, signal when older evidence stops applying: dates alone may not make models adapt reliably [1].
Use reliable temporal metadata, since date-filtered web search can still leak post-cutoff information [2].
Automated community clustering for topic modeling is addressed by several papers that combine clustering/community detection with embeddings and (in some cases) LLM-based steps.

Brady and Islam propose iterative topic taxonomy induction that builds an interpretable hierarchy by clustering documents via embeddings and then using an iterative LLM process to construct and assign consistent topic labels across clusters [4].

Haschka and Bakarji discover multi-scale semantic structure by applying hierarchical density modeling over LLM embeddings, producing a tree that captures how semantic groups merge at progressively relaxed density levels [8].
Haschka and Bakarji’s approach differs from the taxonomy-induction setting of [4] by focusing on multi-resolution hierarchy from data rather than taxonomy induction.

If you specifically mean “communities” via graph-based methods, Saha et al. use a graph of arguments with multiple relationship types (e.g., topic similarity, shared keywords, entities) and then apply community detection to organize argument communities and summarize viewpoint distributions [7].
This differs from embedding-only or hierarchical density trees by emphasizing community detection on an interaction graph rather than topic-label assignment [7].
Zichao Wei’s work connects structural generalization to computational complexity in two ways.

One paper argues that, under the assumption TC⁰ ≠ NC¹, pure Transformers cannot learn structural generalization because the relevant tree-evaluation problem is NC¹-complete, while their learnable class is contained in TC⁰ [1].
Another presents a neural cellular automaton that learns compositional rules from data without hand-written rules and evaluates its structural generalization on SLOG [2].

DeCode, by Po-Jen Ko, Chen-Han Tsai, and Yu-Shao Peng, is a training-free, model-agnostic framework that decouples answer content from delivery to tailor medical QA responses to individual patient contexts.
On OpenAI HealthBench, it improves zero-shot performance from 28.4% to 49.8%, and the authors report state-of-the-art performance against existing methods [1].

For linear-time long-context recall, the Raven paper directly targets the recall problem by changing how a linear model writes to memory: it uses a fixed set of memory slots and learned input-dependent routing so only a selected subset of slots is decayed/updated at each step, aiming to preserve long-range content while avoiding interference from dense state updates and avoiding SWA’s fixed-window eviction.
It reports strong long-context recall on recall-intensive benchmarks and effectiveness when extrapolating to much longer contexts.

[2] These differ from Adaptive Memory Decay for Log-Linear Attention, which focuses on making the Fenwick-tree hierarchy’s decay parameter input-dependent (via an MLP) to adapt memory weighting by content while preserving log-linear complexity.

ViSAR introduces a training-free adaptive-k retrieval method for visual document question answering that dynamically determines how many document pages to retrieve based on the query, aiming to reduce latency while maintaining or improving answer accuracy versus fixed top-k retrieval.

[1] In addition, LAD-RAG uses a layout-aware dynamic RAG approach where an LLM agent adaptively retrieves the necessary evidence pages at inference rather than using a fixed top-k number, improving evidence recall for multi-page reasoning.

[2] D2-ScaleAgent also explicitly targets dynamic scaling at test time by expanding retrieval and pruning evidence based on query difficulty, though it focuses on an agentic retrieval-and-reasoning loop rather than a single page-fetch count rule.

[10] These differ in mechanism: ViSAR changes the retrieved page count directly via a query-conditioned similarity matrix, LAD-RAG adapts retrieval using both neural and symbolic (layout) indices, and D2-ScaleAgent scales retrieval via dynamic routing and an evidence bank.

Different retraction maps affect spherical residual stability mainly through how they turn update magnitude into a rotation angle on the hypersphere.

On the sphere, the papers say all retractions reduce to this single scalar choice; some produce angles that saturate instead of growing without bound, and finite-p angular retractions gave the best validation loss, suggesting the exponential map is not the most stable or preferred choice for spherical residual streams [1].

In particular, projection- and Cayley-based spherical normalizations are exactly norm-preserving and use only algebraic operations, while the exponential map is just one endpoint in the same spectrum [1].

A related result also favors Cayley-style spherical/orthogonal updates for stability: an adaptive Cayley rotation preserves orthogonality for all inputs and achieved the best long-horizon stability among compared residual methods, with strong norm preservation [6].
However, that paper studies orthogonal residual connections more broadly rather than the specific one-parameter spherical retraction family analyzed in [1].

A training-free LLM active-learning framework proposes materials experiments directly from text descriptions in an iterative few-shot setting, without training a task-specific model; it reports reaching top-performing candidates with over 70% fewer experiments than the compared approaches [1].
LLMs can also suggest novel battery-material candidates through analogy-guided reasoning [2].
These approaches select or generate suggestions, but the abstracts do not establish that LLM proposals are automatically reliable; experimental validation remains important.

For robust intent classification in chatbots, the papers point to a few complementary strategies: use models and evaluations that explicitly test perturbation robustness [1], prefer attention pooling over mean pooling when user messages contain conversational noise like greetings or off-topic remarks [2], and consider training-free methods if you expect mixed-intent or adversarial prompts, since they are generally more robust in those settings [3].
For multi-intent spoken interactions, a semantic-frame self-consistency method improves overall accuracy and slot F1, though intent accuracy stays mostly stable [6].

If robustness includes unknown or out-of-scope intents, open-intent methods are relevant: ellipsoid-based decision boundaries improve open intent detection and generalization [4], while uncertainty estimation for open-set text classification helps predict recognition errors and reject unknowns, including on intent datasets [10].
For multilingual customer-service chatbots, translated benchmarks can overestimate robustness on noisy native queries, so realistic native-query evaluation is important [7].

Saahil Mathur and coauthors’ paper is “Retrieval Improvements Do Not Guarantee Better Answers: A Study of RAG for AI Policy QA.” [1] It studies RAG for AI governance and policy analysis using a corpus of AI policy documents, and finds that fine-tuning improves retrieval metrics but does not consistently improve end-to-end QA; stronger retrieval can sometimes produce more confident hallucinations when relevant documents are missing.

For LLM-based popularity prediction in recommendation, TRAIL is the closest match: it fine-tunes an LLM to predict short-term item popularity and produce natural-language explanations, aligning both with structured trend signals [1].

Other papers address related but different problems: one uses LLMs as explainable re-rankers alongside traditional recommenders [2], while another selectively uses LLM pairwise ranking guidance when it is expected to be reliable, including based on item popularity [3].

The closest match is Counter-GEO-Bench: it evaluates defenses against misleading pages that are retrieved and distort generated answers, though its abstract does not describe testing whether removing a page changes the answer [10].
For broader search reliability, another paper measures source credibility and answer groundedness, including the risk of amplifying misinformation from low-credibility sources [9].

To make item IDs change and update automatically during training in a generative search/recommendation system, the papers support using Semantic IDs (SIDs) but carefully managing their drift so already-learned retrieval/generation paths are not disrupted.

One approach is to freeze the SID mappings for existing items while inserting new items, and warm-start the model so updates remain compatible; this “insert new-items, freeze old-items; warm-start when possible” principle helps prevent retrieval degradation from remapping-induced “SID semantic drift.” [1] For user-pattern–aware updates, you can refresh interaction-informed SIDs and then align the refreshed SIDs back to the existing SID vocabulary so the retriever checkpoint stays compatible for warm-start fine-tuning, avoiding full rebuild-and-retrain.

[2] Alternatively, for collaborative tokenizers, drift-aware continual tokenization can identify item-level drift confidence and reassign codes using a relaxed-to-strict strategy to limit unnecessary token changes.

[5] These differ in what they update: [1] focuses on topology preservation under dynamic item arrivals, [2] focuses on aligning refreshed collaborative semantics to prevent staleness, and [5] focuses on continual tokenizer updates guided by drift identification and constrained reassignment.
Yes: several papers propose hierarchical retrieval methods that connect search terms to relevant text chunks through summary trees or tree-like navigation.

DTCRS dynamically builds a summary tree using document structure and query semantics, decomposes the question, and uses sub-question embeddings as cluster centers so summaries are more relevant to the query [2].

RAPTOR-style approaches are also discussed as recursively clustering chunks and ranking summary nodes alongside raw chunks, though one paper argues the gain mainly comes from the tree’s navigation structure rather than the summary content itself [1].
If you want alternatives to LLM-written summaries, NavTree uses a deterministic balanced tree over chunks and performs lexical-and-dense frontier walking to emit relevant leaf chunks [1].
SproutRAG builds a binary chunking tree and uses hierarchical beam search for multi-granularity retrieval without compressed summaries [3].
SVD-RAG keeps the hierarchical tree idea but replaces LLM summaries with extractive SVD-based summarization for cheaper tree construction [9].

One way is prompt-based length tracking: Plan-and-Write proposes a structure-guided prompting method that uses deliberate planning and word counting mechanisms in the prompt to better adhere to specified length constraints without retraining.

It is difficult for neural networks to learn highly ambiguous token distributions because higher ambiguity makes the target next-token distribution harder to represent and fit accurately.

In particular, more ambiguous next-token distributions require more capacity to store, larger embeddings to represent, more optimization steps, and they amplify token-sampling noise, all of which makes accurate learning challenging [1].

Relatedly, when learning involves conditional uncertainty, models may first lock onto easier marginal structure rather than the full conditional distribution; in a controlled setting with K-fold ambiguity, the model learns the marginal first and only later collapses to the full conditional via a sharp transition.
This suggests that ambiguous conditional structure can stabilize simpler, lower-accuracy solutions before the network can represent the full conditional behavior [2].

These effects differ in focus: [1] attributes difficulty directly to ambiguity increasing representational/learning burden and sampling noise, while [2] studies a conditional-learning dynamic where ambiguity produces an initial plateau for the marginal before conditional learning completes.

Related papers are about bidding around LLMs in advertising rather than API request priority.

A related Tannenbaum paper focuses on how request state is distributed across turns, arguing that the final prompt often does not capture the full session context, but it explicitly does not estimate the causal effect of history on model answers [2].

The matching paper is “Rethinking the Role of Efficient Attention in Hybrid Architectures” by Ziqing Qiao and coauthors.

It studies how efficient attention affects hybrid models, reporting that full attention primarily supports long-range retrieval while efficient attention shapes its optimization, and that larger sliding-window attention can delay retrieval-head formation.
It also finds that applying NoPE only to full-attention layers in a small-window hybrid improves long-context performance with little effect on short-context performance.
The matching paper is “Fast and Geometrically Grounded Lorentz Neural Networks” by Robert van der Klis and coauthors.

It proposes a Lorentz linear layer based on a distance-to-hyperplane formulation, aiming to preserve the expected growth of output hyperbolic norms during training, and describes additional efficiency improvements using Lorentzian activation functions and caching.

Related work differs in focus: [1] studies internal length representations, [4] focuses on robust prompt-only prediction under heavy tails, and [5] handles revisable forecasting during agent execution.

The key difference is that the transfer mechanism is moved from the architecture into the representation, rather than claiming ordinary GNNs on their usual KG input will generalize automatically [1].

Related papers here discuss specialized KG foundation models for unseen graphs [4] or scalable KG link prediction on large graphs [5], but they do not show standard vanilla GNNs doing zero-shot prediction on unknown KGs in the same way [4,5].

It is the closest match to using a network of reference answers for one long student paragraph covering several questions [1].

The other papers are about rubric-based grading, short-answer grading, synthetic training data, transparency, or broader educational scoring, but they do not describe this multi-question single-paragraph setting with graph-based reference-answer retrieval [2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10].
The matching paper is Quantum Generator Kernels by Philipp Altmann, Maximilian Mansky, Maximilian Zorn, et al.

[1] It proposes Quantum Generator Kernels (QGKs), a generator-based quantum kernel method built from Variational Generator Groups that merge universal generators into a parameterizable operator to scale coverage of available quantum space.

[1] According to the abstract, the method is motivated by NISQ-era limits on embedding large real-world data, and it aims to avoid shortcomings of hybrid approaches with fixed intermediate embeddings.

[1] It trains a weight vector to parameterize the projection of the generator groups for the current data context, and the reported experiments show superior projection and classification performance versus state-of-the-art quantum and classical kernel approaches, positioning QGK as a versatile framework for quantum machine learning applications.

A direct “GNN proxy for SDP relaxations” is addressed in the Max-Cut setting: Chen, Qian, Morris, et al. propose a Max-Cut-specific graph neural network that acts as a lightweight, validity-preserving neural proxy for the semidefinite programming (SDP) relaxations used inside exact branch-and-bound.
The model predicts both primal- and dual-feasible SDP solutions and yields feasible Max-Cut solutions via the Goemans–Williamson algorithm, allowing it to be plugged into an exact solver framework.
It is trained self-supervised (without requiring solved SDP relaxations as labels) and empirically reduces the cost of bounding by up to 10.6× versus using Mosek.

[2] Qian and Morris study when GNNs can (or cannot) recover SDP solutions, proving negative results for standard GNN architectures on linear SDPs and identifying a more expressive architecture that can emulate updates of a standard first-order solver; it also reports speedups when using learned predictions to warm-start a first-order solver.
This is more about expressivity and optimization recovery than a Max-Cut-style drop-in SDP solver proxy.

The closest match is a set of surveys and systems on code- or script-centered agent infrastructure, rather than a single paper devoted specifically to reviewing programmable scripts as the core structure for reasoning and tool execution.

Code as Agent Harness frames code as the operational substrate for agent reasoning, action, environment modeling, planning, memory, and tool use, and surveys open challenges for executable, verifiable, stateful agent systems [2].

A Comprehensive Survey on Agent Skills also treats reusable procedural artifacts as the operational layer that supports reliable, reusable, composable execution while agents handle higher-level reasoning and planning [3].
For more direct script-like tool execution, The Bitter Lesson of Tool Calling studies programmatic tool calling with typed Python stubs and finds it a viable alternative to JSON tool calls [1].

It builds semantic IDs directly from native LLM vocabulary tokens, lets identifier length adapt to item semantic complexity, and replaces autoregressive SID generation with token-set prediction and token-level item scoring [1].
The abstract says it outperforms strong baselines, improves zero-shot item cold-start, and is much faster at inference than LC-Rec [1].

Related variable-length semantic-ID papers differ in approach: one introduces adaptive-length IDs with a discrete variational autoencoder and Gumbel-Softmax under a probabilistic framework [2]; another learns variable-length tokenization based on item popularity using PIBA, hyperbolic residual quantization, and a soft length controller [3]; and CapsID uses soft capsule routing with confidence-driven SID termination [4].
Feng et al.’s paper proposes recovering a compact, jointly sufficient set of repository evidence for a coding agent’s next decision, conditioned on what the agent has already seen.
Its benchmark and experiments report higher complete-set recovery than similarity-based retrieval, emphasizing set construction over reranking individual passages [1].
Several papers address robust intent classification for chatbots.

Another paper focuses specifically on noise-robust conversational intent classification and finds that attention pooling is better under noisy conditions, while mean pooling can hurt performance [2].
A third study reports that training-based classifiers are better on harder intent tasks, while training-free methods are generally more robust to mixed-intent and adversarial prompts [3].

For broader chatbot settings, one paper proposes an open-intent method with stronger detection of unknown intents and improved open-world robustness [4], and another builds uncertainty estimation for open-set text classification, including intent datasets, to predict when a system will make recognition errors [10].

It specifically reports that domain-specific fine-tuning improves retrieval metrics but can still fail to improve answer quality, and may even increase confident hallucinations when relevant documents are missing [1].
If you meant a broader RAG-for-policy search, this set is otherwise mostly about medical, industrial, financial, multimodal, or general QA rather than policy QA [2-10].

MIC focuses on identifying and explaining inconsistencies between an image and its paired claim, especially for AI-generated images [4].

The strongest match is The Missing Complement: State-Conditioned Minimal Sufficient Evidence for Coding Agents, by Zhexi Feng and coauthors, which is explicitly about recovering “state-conditioned minimal sufficient evidence” for coding agents and framing retrieval as set construction rather than ranking [1].
It studies how to recover a compact evidence combination that supplies what the agent’s next decision still lacks [1].

Related papers also discuss evidence retrieval, but with different goals: ContextBench evaluates context recall, precision, and efficiency in coding agents [4], and Agent Retrieval Bench studies repository context retrieval and selective retrieval for the next needed files [9].
R2LM in Bifocal Diffusion Language Models is designed to improve throughput by combining causal attention with a lightweight reverse Mamba sidecar, while keeping KV caching compatible [1].
The paper reports 2.4× to 12.9× higher throughput than bidirectional diffusion LMs and 1.9× to 2.9× speedup over autoregressive baselines in batch serving with parallel decoding and KV caching [1].

The closest match is decoupled split learning with an auxiliary loss: instead of propagating error signals back across the client-server split, the client uses a local auxiliary classifier for its own error signal while the server trains on transmitted activations with the true loss.
This removes the need to send backward gradients, cutting split-learning communication roughly in half while maintaining performance comparable to standard split learning [1].
Related papers also avoid standard backprop-style credit assignment, but with different goals.

Predictive coding with highway error propagation and Error Diffusion both replace backpropagation with alternative error-routing mechanisms for training deep or biologically constrained networks, rather than focusing on reducing data exchange in shared distributed architectures [5,7].
Other communication-efficient work here mainly compresses gradients, weight updates, or critic parameters instead of avoiding error-signal propagation altogether [2,4,10].

Repeating training data can hurt pretraining performance when it creates too much duplication: one study finds that eval loss peaks at an intermediate repeat count, and that repeating a moderate subset a moderate number of times can damage performance more than either many repeats of a small subset or a few repeats of a large subset [1].
It also reports that the most damaging repeat count changes with model size, and that certain repetition settings can waste a large share of compute compared with no repetition [1].
Other papers show the effect is not always purely negative.

With limited unique data, one study finds that more epochs can improve pretraining outcomes, and that factors like shard order, concentrating repeats, and source entropy change the loss penalty from repetition [2].
Another finds that repeating standard pre-training data can support strong downstream performance for a diffusion language model, even as validation cross-entropy rises [10].
Make user goals explicit rather than inferring them only from clicks or item transitions.
Use comments and reviews to capture why someone chose an item, and model motivation and high-level intents to guide recommendations and make them more interpretable [1, 2, 4].
Distinguish a user’s current demand from the policy for what to recommend or avoid, then refine that policy using outcome feedback [10].
Natural-language profiles can also let users state and edit preferences directly, though systems need to be evaluated on whether they actually follow those instructions [9].
Repeating training data during pretraining usually hurts base-model performance relative to using fresh data, especially when unique data is the bottleneck [1, 2, 3].

The damage is systematic: exact-document repetition can create a worst-case intermediate repeat count, can waste a substantial fraction of compute, and tends to increase memorization while degrading generalization [1].
With finite unique-document pools, the loss penalty is mild for small models but grows quickly for larger models, including for semantically redundant data as models become more capable [3].
How much repetition hurts depends on how it is done [2].
A second epoch is nearly as valuable as a fresh one, but repeated tokens become much less valuable after a critical epoch count; larger models tolerate fewer epochs when the corpus is fixed [2].
Repeat structure also matters: consecutive shard replay and concentrating repeats on fewer samples both raise loss [2].
One exception is diffusion language models: under limited unique data, they can outperform autoregressive models by training for more epochs on repeated data [10].
Yes — the closest match is “MiniFool -- Physics-Constraint-Aware Minimizer-Based Adversarial Attacks in Deep Neural Networks,” by Lucie Flek and colleagues.

It presents physics-inspired adversarial attacks for particle and astroparticle physics, using a cost function that combines a chi-squared-based test statistic with deviation from a target score, and it studies robustness under experimental-uncertainty constraints [1].

A related paper by the same first author, “Uncovering Hidden Systematics in Neural Network Models for High Energy Physics,” also looks at perturbations consistent with experimental uncertainties, but its focus is on probing hidden sensitivity and systematic uncertainty rather than introducing a new attack algorithm [8].

WIND presents a single pre-trained foundation model for “zero-shot atmospheric modeling” that replaces specialized baselines across a wide range of weather and climate tasks, framed as inverse problems solved via posterior sampling, without any task-specific fine-tuning [1].
It supports diverse tasks including probabilistic forecasting, spatial/temporal downscaling, reconstruction from sparse observations, and enforcing global dry air mass conservation [1].
The matching paper is “Structural Segmentation for Brazilian Legal Document Retrieval” by Leandro Carísio Fernandes and coauthors.
It studies splitting Brazilian legal acts into structurally organized chunks for retrieval, comparing hierarchical segmentation with simpler article- and component-based chunks.

Structural segmentation improves dense retrieval over whole-document indexing, but does not consistently help lexical retrieval; core chunks enriched with document metadata perform comparably to or better than the full hierarchy.
Automated community clustering for topic modeling is addressed by several papers that combine clustering/community detection with embeddings and (in some cases) LLM-based steps.

Brady and Islam propose iterative topic taxonomy induction that builds an interpretable hierarchy by clustering documents via embeddings and then using an iterative LLM process to construct and assign consistent topic labels across clusters [4].

Haschka and Bakarji discover multi-scale semantic structure by applying hierarchical density modeling over LLM embeddings, producing a tree that captures how semantic groups merge at progressively relaxed density levels [8].
Haschka and Bakarji’s approach differs from the taxonomy-induction setting of [4] by focusing on multi-resolution hierarchy from data rather than taxonomy induction.

If you specifically mean “communities” via graph-based methods, Saha et al. use a graph of arguments with multiple relationship types (e.g., topic similarity, shared keywords, entities) and then apply community detection to organize argument communities and summarize viewpoint distributions [7].
This differs from embedding-only or hierarchical density trees by emphasizing community detection on an interaction graph rather than topic-label assignment [7].
Yes: several papers describe improving AI with self-generated feedback instead of human labels, including for following complex rules.

RuleEvolve directly targets rules for coding agents by mutating candidate rules and using a judge module to evaluate and keep the best ones, outperforming manual rule engineering and prompt optimization baselines [10].
More broadly, self-improvement frameworks let models generate data, evaluate outputs, and iteratively refine capabilities with minimal or no external supervision [4].
If you mean self-feedback during reasoning or agent behavior, there are a few variants.
TRT uses self-generated verification signals at test time to improve answers without external feedback [1].
CoNL uses multi-agent critique and meta-evaluation, rewarding critiques that help improve solutions, so generation and judging improve together without external judges or ground truth [8].
NRT trains reasoning models from standard question-answer pairs by having the model generate its own reasoning traces, avoiding expert-written demonstrations and external verifiers [5].
For prompts whose responses can vary widely in length, the most directly relevant paper treats output length as a prompt-conditioned distribution rather than a single fixed target.
It proposes using repeated generations to train either a robust median point estimate or a distributional estimate that preserves uncertainty [4].

Another paper reports that an LLM’s hidden state at the end of the prompt contains a linearly decodable estimate of the eventual response length, though this is an approximate estimate, not exact counting [1].

Koh et al. propose “Continual Post-training Small Models via Synthetic Self-distillation,” introducing Synthetic Self-distillation (SynthSelf) to enable self-distillation for smaller models in continual learning when standard self-distillation relies on strong in-context learning.

SynthSelf imitates in-distribution rewrite by outsourcing the task to a minimally larger same-family aligner, and uses off-policy supervision plus rejection sampling to provide high-quality supervision without breaking the model’s original distribution.
Evaluations report SynthSelf consistently outperforming multiple off- and on-policy distillation methods across small-model scales, including acquisition and retention benchmarks.

[1] Other results focus on different self-distillation settings rather than Koh-style synthetic self-distillation for continual post-training: on-policy self-distillation without supervision (using internal consistency) is studied in U-OPSD [4]; token selection for on-policy self-distillation is addressed by bilevel Top-K selection (BiToK-SD) [5]; and self-distillation for diffusion language models uses masking-mode bidirectional KD (SelFusion) [2].
These differ in task/setting and mechanisms.
Content creators can better understand lack of recommendations by getting transparency into how their specific items influence exposure in recommendation lists.

One approach trains a surrogate (proxy) model to approximate a recommender’s item exposure distribution and then attributes which features most drive exposure (or non-exposure) across the whole user base, helping providers see factors behind recommendation outcomes at the system level [1].
Several inference-time strategies target different weaknesses in multimodal LLM decoding.

For diffusion-based multimodal models, IGFD prioritizes useful semantic anchors, VRCD selects tokens with complementary visual grounding, and Context-Aware Cluster Decoding favors tokens supported by nearby context [1–3].
STDec uses spatial and temporal stability to improve throughput while maintaining comparable task performance [7].
For reducing hallucinations, causal decoding intervenes on generation dynamics to curb unsupported object mentions, while LIME shifts relevance toward perceptual input [4, 9].
A survey organizes broader LLM and vision-language decoding methods into token-level, sequence-level, and parallel-generation paradigms [5].
Yes.

The supplied papers support blocking fake or distorted external-search information by testing counterfactual retrieval conditions, especially removing or refusing suspect pages and seeing whether the agent abstains or changes its answer.

One paper directly removes gold passages from the index and shows that when the retrieval tool explicitly refuses instead of returning irrelevant text, compliant agents sharply increase abstention on unanswerable questions and cut wrong answers almost one-for-one; it also notes that the main bottleneck is detecting when to trigger that refusal [6].

Another paper proposes a benchmark for defenses against misinformation injected through generative-engine-optimized pages, showing that standard guardrails help little while a benchmark baseline can substantially reduce attack success with near-zero utility loss [10].
Paper [1] directly addresses how efficient-attention modules shape hybrid architectures, analyzing scaling and mechanisms.

It finds efficient-attention design mainly affects how fast long-context capability emerges, and that long-range retrieval is carried by full attention while efficient attention shapes the optimization trajectory, including the “Large-Window Laziness” effect where larger SWA windows can delay retrieval head formation in full-attention layers.
It also proposes improving long-context performance by applying NoPE only to full-attention layers in a small-window SWA hybrid.

If you instead meant a hybrid architecture efficiently combining attention types for long-context reasoning, paper [2] introduces Ring-linear models that integrate linear attention and softmax attention to reduce I/O and computation overhead, and explores the ratio between the attention mechanisms to find an optimal structure.
Paper [5] focuses on principled head-level hybrid design separating retrieval and positional heads using intervention metrics and instantiating a head-wise hybrid architecture.
Large language models can actively gather information for better product recommendations mainly through conversational preference elicitation and dynamic retrieval.

In conversational systems, LLMs can ask users targeted questions to collect informative preference cues; the best questions depend on dialogue stage, with attribute-based questions working better early and item-based questions becoming more effective later [5].
They can also choose interactions that maximize information gain by reducing uncertainty over recommendations, improving both recommendation quality and conversational efficiency [8].
Beyond asking users directly, LLM-based recommenders can gather richer context from behavior and catalog data.

They can generate real-time natural-language user personas that combine known interests with novel topics to balance exploitation and exploration [2], infer latent intent and item relationships from metadata to enrich recommendation inputs [1], and operate over live e-commerce catalogues using self-refreshing retrieval so recommendations reflect newly added, changed, or deleted products [7].
These approaches differ: [5,8] focus on interactive information gathering from the user, while [1,2,7] focus on enriching or refreshing the system’s available information.

The closest match is POLO, a partially observable multi-agent reinforcement learning framework for dispatching optimization in multi-platform instant delivery systems, where couriers are not exclusive to one platform and each platform only observes its own orders and courier interactions due to privacy and operational constraints [2].
It learns dispatch policies from platform-local observations and is designed to work with incomplete courier information [2].

If you mean a broader delivery-routing setting rather than multiple apps/platforms, other papers focus on ride-sharing dispatch with many drivers [1], last-mile pickup dispatch and routing [7], or multi-vehicle pickup-delivery [3], but they do not specifically frame the problem as multiple apps with partial visibility into all driver data [1, 3, 7].
The closest matches are papers on adaptive chunking and structure-aware retrieval for RAG.

Intent-Driven Dynamic Chunking and SmartChunk both adapt chunk boundaries or abstraction levels to user queries, which can help a bot answer questions from long technical documents more accurately [1, 9].

LARAG, Adaptive Chunking, and the EDA function-aware retrieval paper go further by using document structure, metadata, or functional units to retrieve more relevant evidence from technical documentation [2, 3, 6].
